cards.title: 2.1 The Nature and Balancing of Oxidation-Reduction Reactions
body: 2.1 The Nature and Balancing of Oxidation-Reduction Reactions

**Oxidation-Reduction (Redox) Reaction** is defined as a chemical process involving the transfer of electrons between reacting chemical species, characterized by simultaneous changes in the oxidation numbers of the atoms involved.

Historically, the understanding of redox chemistry evolved through three distinct conceptual stages. In the traditional era, chemists defined oxidation simply as the chemical addition of oxygen to a substance or the removal of hydrogen from it. Conversely, reduction was viewed as the addition of hydrogen or the removal of oxygen. While this traditional framework remains useful for describing basic combustion and organic metabolic pathways, it is fundamentally limited because many chemical reactions display identical physical and electronic characteristics without involving a single atom of

cards.title: Oxidation-Reduction Reactions
body: To apply redox principles to complex covalent molecules where outright electron transfer is incomplete, chemists developed the oxidation number method. An oxidation number is the formal electrical charge assigned to an atom in a given compound, representing the number of electrons lost or gained (either completely or partially) by that atom to form the compound. This method is governed by a strict set of IUPAC rules: any free element in its standard state has an oxidation number of exactly zero; simple monoatomic ions have an oxidation number equal to their ionic charge; hydrogen is assigned $$+1$$ (except in metal hydrides where it is $$-1$$); oxygen is assigned $$-2$$ (except in peroxides where it is $$-1$$ and superoxides where it is $$-1/2$$); and the sum of all oxidation numbers in a neutral compound must equal zero, while in polyatomic ions, the sum must equal the net charge of the

body: Balancing these equations cannot always be accomplished by simple inspection because both mass and electrical charge must be conserved simultaneously. Chemists utilize two systematic approaches: the Oxidation Number Change Method and the Ion-Electron (Half-Reaction) Method. The half-reaction method is highly favored for aqueous chemistry. It involves splitting the overall redox equation into two separate half-reactions: an oxidation half-reaction and a reduction half-reaction. Each half-reaction is balanced individually for mass (balancing non-O and non-H elements first, then adding $$H_2O$$ to balance oxygen, and $$H^+$$ to balance hydrogen) and then balanced for charge by adding electrons ($$e^-$$). To overcome these limitations, the electron transfer method was established. Under this framework, oxidation is redefined as the loss of one or more electrons from a chemical species, while reduction is the gain of one or more electrons. A classic example of this process is the reaction between elemental sodium and chlorine gas to form sodium chloride. Here, each sodium atom loses an electron to become a sodium cation, undergoing oxidation, while each chlorine atom gains an electron to become a chloride anion, undergoing reduction. This conceptual shift is summarized by the widely used mnemonic **OILRIG** (Oxidation Is Loss, Reduction Is Gain).

cards.title: Oxidation-Reduction Reactions
body: Using these assigned oxidation numbers, we can easily classify the reactants. An **oxidizing agent** (or oxidant) is defined as an electron acceptor that oxidizes another substance and, in doing so, undergoes reduction itself (its oxidation number decreases). A **reducing agent** (or reductant) is an electron donor that reduces another substance and, in the process, undergoes oxidation itself (its oxidation number increases). For example, when metallic iron reacts with copper(II) sulfate, iron reduces the copper ions to metallic copper while being oxidized to iron(II) sulfate. Here, iron is the reducing agent, and the copper(II) ion is the oxidizing agent.

body:
| Definition Method | Oxidation | Reduction | Scope of Application |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Traditional Method** | Addition of oxygen; removal of hydrogen | Removal of oxygen; addition of hydrogen | Limited to oxygen and hydrogen reactions |
| **Electron Transfer Method** | Loss of electrons ($$\\text{e}^-$$) | Gain of electrons ($$\\text{e}^-$$) | Limited to ionic and basic transfer reactions |
| **Oxidation Number Method** | Increase in oxidation number | Decrease in oxidation number | Universally applicable to all chemical reactions |

> **💡 Did You Know?**: Fireflies produce their characteristic biological light through a highly efficient enzymatic redox reaction. An organic molecule called luciferin undergoes oxidation catalyzed by the enzyme luciferase, converting chemical energy directly into light with nearly $$100\\%$$ efficiency and producing zero waste heat!

### 📝 Topic Challenge (Moderate to Hard)
1. Determine the oxidation number of sulfur ($$S$$) in the thiosulfate ion ($$S_2O_3^{2-}$$).
*Answer:* Let $$x$$ be the oxidation number of $$S$$. The oxidation number of oxygen is $$-2$$. The sum of the oxidation numbers in the polyatomic ion must equal its charge ($$-2$$). Therefore: $$2(x) + 3(-2) = -2 \\implies 2x - 6 = -2 \\implies 2x = +4 \\implies x = +2$$. The oxidation number of sulfur is **$$+2$$**.

cards.title: 2.2 Electrolysis and Faraday's Laws
body: 2.2 Electrolysis and Faraday's Laws

**Electrolysis** is defined as the chemical decomposition of an electrolyte caused by the passage of a direct electric current (DC) through it in an electrolytic cell, thereby driving non-spontaneous chemical reactions.

To conduct electrolysis, an apparatus known as an electrolytic cell is assembled. This cell consists of three primary components: an electrolyte, a pair of conductive electrodes, and an external direct current (DC) electrical source. The electrolyte is a substance containing free-moving ions, which can be either a molten ionic salt or an aqueous ionic solution. Solids cannot act as electrolytes because their ions are locked in a rigid crystal lattice and cannot migrate to carry an electrical charge.
When the DC power source is activated, it pumps electrons through the external circuit, creating oppositely charged electrodes. The

cards.title: Oxidation-Reduction Reactions
body: When a molten binary salt such as molten lead bromide ($$PbBr_2$$) is electrolyzed, the results are straightforward. At the cathode, lead ions ($$Pb^{2+}$$) gain electrons to deposit as liquid lead metal: $$Pb^{2+}(l) + 2e^- \\rightarrow Pb(s)$$. At the anode, bromide ions ($$Br^-$$) lose electrons to form reddish-brown bromine gas: $$2Br^-(l) \\rightarrow Br_2(g) + 2e^-$$. However, when aqueous solutions are electrolyzed, water molecules also dissociate ($$H^+$$ and $$OH^-$$) and compete with the salt ions. The selection of which ion is discharged at each electrode is dictated by three primary factors: the position of the ions in the electrochemical series, the relative concentration of the ions in the solution, and the chemical nature of the electrodes used.

cards.title: Study Notes worked
cards.problem: During the electrolysis of molten lead bromide ($$PbBr_2$$), what product is formed at the negative cathode?

steps.text: **Step 1: Identify ions present in molten lead bromide**
The molten state contains only $$Pb^{2+}$$ and $$Br^-$$ ions.
**Step 2: Determine which ion migrates to the negative cathode**
Cations (positively charged) migrate to the negative cathode. Thus, $$Pb^{2+}$$ migrates to the cathode.
**Step 3: Determine the reaction at the cathode**
At the cathode, reduction occurs: $$Pb^{2+} + 2e^- \\rightarrow Pb(s)$$.

cards.title: Study Notes worked
cards.problem: Which of the following compounds behaves as a weak electrolyte when dissolved in water?

steps.text: Strong electrolytes dissociate completely. Weak electrolytes dissociate partially. Non-electrolytes do not dissociate.
$$HCl$$ and $$NaOH$$ dissociate completely (strong electrolytes). $$C_{12}H_{22}O_{11}$$ does not dissociate (non-electrolyte). Acetic acid ($$CH_3COOH$$) dissociates only partially.

cards.problem: During the electrolysis of dilute sulfuric acid ($$H_2SO_4$$) using platinum electrodes, which gas is liberated at the positive anode?

steps.text: **Step 1: Identify anions competing at the anode**
The anions present are $$SO_4^{2-}$$ and $$OH^-$$ (from water).
$$OH^-$$ is much lower in the electrochemical series than $$SO_4^{2-}$$, meaning it is far more easily discharged.
